title: airDash purpose
definition: airDash is the virtual-airline website, rules engine, and durable operational record.
why: A contributor must preserve the reason the platform exists rather than optimize isolated code.
outcomes: Explain the coordination problem airDash solves.
Distinguish product behavior from documentation or automation.

title: Actors and roles
definition: Visitors, signed-in users, active pilots, the owner, automation, and background jobs have distinct capabilities.
why: Correct reasoning begins with who acts and which boundary grants permission.
outcomes: Map an action to the actor that performs it.
Identify the role required for a workflow.

title: Core flight workflow
definition: The core workflow runs from sign-in and application through booking, dispatch, report, review, and updated state.
why: The workflow connects otherwise isolated pages, routes, tables, and side effects.
outcomes: Trace all seven workflow stages.
Name the route and durable side effect at each stage.

title: Scope and project status
definition: The platform supports one airline, one owner, Discord authentication, BCS3 aircraft, and one production environment.
why: Unsupported assumptions produce incorrect features and unsafe operating plans.
outcomes: State supported and unsupported use.
Explain how the single-environment status affects validation.

title: Canonical documentation and evidence
definition: Architecture, API, data model, and configuration are canonical references; academy levels report evidence with explicit limits.
why: A learner must know where facts live and avoid mistaking completion labels for professional certification.
outcomes: Choose the canonical page for a changed contract.
Explain what academy evidence can and cannot prove.

title: Files, directories, and paths
definition: Files hold bytes; directories organize them; absolute and relative paths resolve from different starting points.
why: Every command and source reference depends on the correct working directory.
outcomes: Distinguish absolute, relative, home, and parent paths.
Resolve a project path from a stated working directory.

title: Permissions, executables, processes, services, and signals
definition: Permissions control file access; processes run programs; services supervise long-running processes; signals request lifecycle changes.
why: Build output must be readable by Nginx and the API must shut down cleanly under PM2.
outcomes: Interpret common permission modes.
Trace SIGTERM through the API shutdown sequence.

title: Standard streams and exit codes
definition: stdin supplies input, stdout carries normal results, stderr carries diagnostics, and exit code zero indicates success.
why: Validation and automation use stream separation and exit codes to decide whether work passed.
outcomes: Predict where redirected output goes.
Use an exit code rather than visual output as the primary result.

title: Ports, localhost, and environment variables
definition: Ports identify listeners; localhost stays on the machine; environment variables configure a process at startup.
why: The API, auth service, Vite, and PostgreSQL depend on distinct ports and startup configuration.
outcomes: Map each project service to its port.
Explain process environment, .env, and code-default precedence.

title: Shell syntax and command safety
definition: Quoting, expansion, pipes, redirection, backgrounding, and subshells change command behavior and blast radius.
why: A malformed or destructive command can alter production, expose output, or leave orphan processes.
outcomes: Explain a documented command token by token.
Choose a non-destructive inspection before a mutation.

title: Required tools and versions
definition: Node.js, npm, Git, PostgreSQL, Docker, Python, and PowerShell have documented roles and version constraints.
why: A reproducible environment starts by proving the exact executable and version in use.
outcomes: Identify which tools are required or optional.
Interpret an engine-version failure.

title: Dependency installation
definition: npm ci restores the exact lock-file tree and refuses manifest-lock disagreement.
why: Using the reproducible installer prevents silent dependency drift.
outcomes: Distinguish npm ci from npm install.
Predict files read and written by dependency installation.

title: Local PostgreSQL setup
definition: A local PostgreSQL 16 database can run natively or in a loopback-only Docker container.
why: API development requires an isolated database rather than production data.
outcomes: Explain the Docker port and volume flags.
Verify readiness and schema count safely.

title: Local environment file
definition: api/.env supplies local database, authentication, owner, port, SimBrief, and optional VAPID configuration and must remain untracked.
why: Correct local configuration enables the API without spreading production secrets.
outcomes: Construct a safe local environment template.
Explain why placeholders and production values differ.

title: Local process topology
definition: A complete local environment uses PostgreSQL, a loopback mock auth server, the API, and Vite.
why: A learner must start, verify, and stop each process without confusing local and production state.
outcomes: Name all local processes and verification calls.
Diagnose a port or working-directory startup failure.

title: Repository, working tree, staging, and commits
definition: Git separates tracked history, current files, staged changes, and immutable commits.
why: Safe review depends on knowing which state a command changes.
outcomes: Explain status before and after staging.
Select a command that preserves or discards the intended layer.

title: Branches and remotes
definition: A branch names a commit line; origin names the GitHub copy; fetch, pull, and push move information differently.
why: Contributions must remain isolated from release branches and remote state must be explicit.
outcomes: Distinguish fetch, pull, and push.
Create and publish a feature branch safely.

title: Status, diff, log, and blame evidence
definition: Read-only Git commands reveal file state, changes, and history before any mutation.
why: Inspection first prevents accidental staging and incorrect recovery.
outcomes: Choose the command for unstaged, staged, or historical changes.
Use evidence to identify what changed without rewriting history.

title: Merge conflicts, pull requests, and review
definition: Conflicts require an explicit correct final file; pull requests record a diff, evidence, and review before merge.
why: Team safety comes from inspectable change and independent review, not only local success.
outcomes: Resolve conflict markers correctly.
Prepare review evidence and respond with new commits.

title: Safe and destructive Git recovery
definition: restore and unstage can preserve work; reset --hard, clean, force push, and branch deletion can destroy it.
why: Recovery commands can irreversibly remove uncommitted or remote work.
outcomes: Choose the least destructive recovery operation.
State when explicit confirmation is required.

title: Values, types, variables, expressions, and functions
definition: JavaScript values have runtime types; functions receive parameters, apply expressions, and return values.
why: These mechanics explain every helper and handler in the API.
outcomes: Trace clean(value, maximum).
Predict a function result from project inputs.

title: Objects, arrays, destructuring, and control flow
definition: Objects name fields, arrays order values, destructuring extracts them, and control flow selects or repeats work.
why: Routes assemble JSON, parallel results, and state transitions with these constructs.
outcomes: Read an object and destructuring expression.
Predict an early return or loop side effect.

title: Modules, imports, exports, and Node.js ESM
definition: ECMAScript modules expose selected names, resolve project paths, and execute top-level startup code in Node.js.
why: Import direction defines architecture, testability, and startup order.
outcomes: Distinguish bare and relative imports.
Explain why .js extensions appear in API imports.

title: Promises, async/await, concurrency, and cleanup
definition: Promises represent future results; await suspends one async function; Promise.all runs independent work concurrently.
why: Database, HTTP, and filesystem operations rely on correct ordering and cleanup.
outcomes: Trace authenticatedUser across success and failure.
Choose sequential or parallel waiting based on dependency.

title: Errors, try/catch/finally, optional chaining, nullish coalescing, and template strings
definition: JavaScript expresses failure, cleanup, absent data, defaults, and formatted output with explicit operators.
why: Correct error propagation protects data and prevents internal detail leakage.
outcomes: Explain a transaction catch/finally path.
Distinguish || from ?? in a project default.

title: Type annotations, interfaces, unions, and nullability
definition: TypeScript describes value shapes and forces explicit handling of optional and nullable data.
why: Frontend changes should fail at type check rather than at runtime.
outcomes: Read an interface and union.
Choose optional, nullable, or required fields for an API response.

title: Generics and the typed API client
definition: api<T> uses a generic response type while ApiError carries a status and readable message.
why: The fetch boundary must preserve cookies, headers, JSON parsing, and typed expectations.
outcomes: Trace api<MeResponse>.
Explain where runtime validation is still absent.

title: JSX, components, props, and rendering
definition: JSX combines markup and expressions; components receive typed props and return renderable nodes.
why: Most airDash interface changes modify component composition rather than raw HTML.
outcomes: Explain punctuation in a project JSX example.
Fix a ReactNode versus string prop mismatch.

title: State, effects, context, and client routing
definition: React state triggers rendering, effects synchronize external work, context shares state, and BrowserRouter selects pages.
why: Incorrect dependencies or route assumptions cause stale data and broken direct navigation.
outcomes: Trace AppContext and refresh.
Diagnose an effect or routing failure.

title: CSS, browser storage, and accessibility
definition: The frontend uses one stylesheet, semantic controls, local storage for non-authoritative UI state, and reduced-motion support.
why: Visual changes must remain keyboard, screen-reader, and motion accessible without moving authoritative state into the browser.
outcomes: Distinguish server and browser state.
Evaluate an interactive control for accessibility.

title: Direct, transitive, runtime, and development dependencies
definition: Manifests name direct dependencies; lock files include transitive packages; runtime and development roles differ.
why: Dependency scope determines installation, production exposure, and review.
outcomes: Classify project packages.
Trace why a type package is development-only.

title: Manifests, lock files, semantic versions, and exact pins
definition: package.json declares intent, package-lock.json fixes the full tree, and airDash pins exact versions.
why: Exact, reviewed changes reduce drift and supply-chain surprise.
outcomes: Interpret major, minor, and patch.
Explain why both manifest and lock file change together.

title: Reproducible installation and supply-chain risk
definition: npm ci verifies and restores the locked tree; dependency names and updates require scrutiny.
why: Installed code executes with developer privileges and can affect builds.
outcomes: Choose a safe installation or update workflow.
Identify a typosquatting or integrity risk.

title: Type checking, compilation, bundling, minification, and content hashes
definition: TypeScript checks types and Vite emits browser JavaScript and CSS with content-derived names.
why: A hash proves artifact content and supports cache-safe publication.
outcomes: Trace the web build steps.
Explain why a source change may create a new bundle name.

title: Editable source versus generated and operational artifacts
definition: web/src is editable, site/app-assets is generated, and site/downloads contains operational files a build must preserve.
why: Editing or deleting the wrong layer loses work or published downloads.
outcomes: Choose the correct file to edit.
Explain emptyOutDir false and the danger of overriding it.

title: Clients, servers, DNS, IP addresses, ports, and TCP
definition: Names resolve to addresses; TCP connects client and server ports; localhost remains on one machine.
why: The production and local topologies depend on understanding each address and listener.
outcomes: Trace a domain to a listener.
Diagnose connection refused versus an HTTP error.

title: TLS, HTTPS, HTTP requests, and responses
definition: TLS protects transport to Caddy; HTTP exchanges method, path, headers, body, status, and response body.
why: Every API and static request crosses this contract.
outcomes: Identify each request and response part.
Explain where encryption begins and ends.

title: HTTP methods, status codes, headers, bodies, and JSON
definition: Methods express intent, status codes classify results, headers carry metadata, and JSON carries structured bodies.
why: Clients and operators must distinguish validation, authorization, conflict, dependency, and server failures.
outcomes: Map project errors to status families.
Predict how the API client handles a non-JSON or non-2xx body.

title: Cookies, sessions, origins, CORS, and CSRF
definition: The browser carries a parent-domain session cookie; Origin identifies the caller and mutation middleware rejects unapproved origins.
why: Authentication alone does not prevent another site from causing an authenticated mutation.
outcomes: Trace session-cookie validation.
Explain why the origin check runs globally before route authorization.

title: API paths, Caddy prefix stripping, pagination, idempotency, and rate limits
definition: Browsers call /api paths, Caddy strips the prefix, some lists paginate, repeated operations differ in safety, and no rate limiter exists.
why: Correct clients and debugging depend on the boundary between public path and Express path.
outcomes: Trace /api/me to /me.
Diagnose the Vite proxy mismatch and reason about retry safety.

title: Express application, middleware order, and route handlers
definition: Global middleware parses and protects a request before route-specific authorization and handler logic.
why: Changing order can bypass controls or alter errors.
outcomes: List middleware in order.
Trace one route from match through response.

title: Authentication, authorization classes, and record ownership
definition: The auth service establishes identity; middleware grants user or owner access; SQL predicates enforce record ownership.
why: A hidden button is not an authorization control and an object ID must not grant access.
outcomes: Distinguish requireUser, requireOwner, pilot checks, and ownership predicates.
Identify the correct boundary for a new route.

title: Input validation and the API error contract
definition: Text cleaning, allow-lists, patterns, numeric bounds, and generic unexpected-error messages protect handlers.
why: Unvalidated input corrupts state or leaks internals; readable deliberate errors support clients.
outcomes: Choose validators for a body field.
Distinguish a deliberate 4xx from an unexpected 500.

title: Parameterized SQL, transactions, row locks, and cleanup
definition: User values use $n parameters; related writes share BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK; FOR UPDATE coordinates concurrency; finally releases clients.
why: These mechanisms jointly prevent injection and partial or racing state.
outcomes: Identify unsafe SQL construction.
Trace booking rollback and unique-index conflict behavior.

title: Route classes, API client behavior, and side effects
definition: Public, user, pilot, and owner routes have documented inputs, response contracts, and durable side effects.
why: A correct change updates handler, consumer type, tests, API reference, and security classification together.
outcomes: Find a route and its consumer.
Plan a backward-compatible response change.

title: Persistent relational data, schemas, tables, rows, columns, and types
definition: PostgreSQL stores durable rows in 15 tables under the airdash schema in the shared dashyden database.
why: Data modeling and inspection require exact entity and type knowledge.
outcomes: Explain schema-qualified tables.
Choose an appropriate project data type and nullability.

title: Primary keys, foreign keys, logical relationships, and deletion behavior
definition: Keys identify and connect rows; some relationships are enforced by PostgreSQL and others by handlers.
why: Deletion and joins behave differently when a relationship is only logical.
outcomes: Read the entity relationship diagram.
Predict a blocked, cascading, or application-controlled deletion.

title: Constraints, partial unique indexes, and invariants
definition: CHECK, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, foreign keys, and partial unique indexes enforce valid state and concurrency-safe business rules.
why: Application checks improve errors; database constraints provide final correctness under races.
outcomes: Explain one active assignment per pilot and aircraft.
Diagnose a 23505 conflict.

title: Transactions, isolation, row locks, and the connection pool
definition: The pool reuses connections; transactions require one dedicated client and read-committed isolation plus explicit locks.
why: Incorrect pooling or cleanup can split atomic work or exhaust connections.
outcomes: Choose pool.query or pool.connect.
Explain FOR UPDATE and finally release.

title: Idempotent migrations, seed data, entity lifecycles, and backup limits
definition: migrate creates and alters schema in file order, seeds reference data, and encodes status lifecycles without versioned rollback.
why: Schema changes can partially apply and source rollback does not reverse them.
outcomes: Design an additive idempotent change.
Trace assignment, report, and aircraft lifecycle effects.

title: System context, components, containers, host processes, ports, mounts, and volumes
definition: Caddy, Nginx, PM2 API, auth, PostgreSQL, browsers, and Windows automation have distinct responsibilities and dependencies.
why: Operation and failure diagnosis begin with the exact runtime topology.
outcomes: Draw every node and connection.
Identify the component that owns a symptom.

title: End-to-end request and data flow
definition: A browser request crosses Caddy, global middleware, authentication, handlers, PostgreSQL, and the typed client.
why: Tracing order reveals where a failure or security decision occurs.
outcomes: Trace GET /api/me.
Locate the boundary responsible for a status code.

title: Startup, shutdown, and process supervision
definition: Startup migrates and repairs before listening; SIGTERM stops push, closes HTTP, ends the pool, and exits; PM2 supervises the process.
why: Deployment and recovery depend on readiness and graceful termination.
outcomes: Order startup and shutdown steps.
Predict PM2 behavior after a startup failure.

title: Background jobs, failure propagation, retries, and silent errors
definition: Expiry, schedule, and push jobs run in process; dependency failures propagate differently and some timer errors are discarded.
why: Silent or crashing failure modes require effect-based verification and explicit operator action.
outcomes: Verify each job by its effects.
Predict behavior during database, auth, provider, or push failure.

title: Trust boundaries, scaling constraints, and architectural tradeoffs
definition: Validation occurs at changing trust levels; single-process jobs and local files constrain horizontal scaling; tradeoffs are explicit.
why: Adding a component or instance without preserving assumptions can duplicate work or expose data.
outcomes: Map every trust boundary.
Evaluate a proposed second API instance.

title: Root and API ownership
definition: Root configuration and api files separate package contracts, scripts, entry point, database, authentication, integrations, and pure modules.
why: A change must land in the owning handwritten file and invoke the right validation.
outcomes: Explain every root and API directory.
Find the module responsible for a backend behavior.

title: Frontend ownership and entry flow
definition: web/index.html and main.tsx mount App; App and extracted modules own pages, types, integrations, and styles.
why: Searching visible text, route tables, types, and CSS locates user-facing behavior.
outcomes: Trace the frontend entry.
Find a page, API call, type, and style.

title: Documentation, scripts, simulator packages, and automation ownership
definition: docs contains canonical prose; scripts, gsx, and livery-templates contain build and Windows automation sources.
why: Specialized artifacts require platform-specific validation and documentation triggers.
outcomes: Choose the owning directory for a simulator or documentation change.
Distinguish source copy from deployed Windows copy.

title: Handwritten, generated, ignored, and operational files
definition: site and node_modules are untracked; app-assets are generated; downloads and profiles are operational; public assets have a source copy.
why: Editing, emptying, or staging the wrong path loses work or data.
outcomes: Classify representative paths.
Choose backup and edit procedures for each class.

title: Search and execution-path tracing
definition: Visible text, route strings, symbols, types, queries, and side effects form an inspectable path through the repository.
why: A contributor should locate behavior from evidence rather than framework convention or guesswork.
outcomes: Use grep to locate a feature.
Trace booking from click to audit event and response.

title: Application, pilot approval, and assignment lifecycle
definition: A signed-in user applies, the owner approves a numbered pilot, and the pilot books one active assignment.
why: Identity, role, route, aircraft, status, and deadlines establish all later flight state.
outcomes: Trace onboarding writes.
Apply one-pilot and one-aircraft active invariants.

title: Flight Board, gate allocation, start, cancellation, and dispatch
definition: Booking selects an available aircraft and gates; the Hangar starts or cancels and integrates SimBrief, Volanta, and VATSIM.
why: Operational consistency requires owner, status, route, aircraft, gate, and deadline validation.
outcomes: Trace booking and cancellation side effects.
Diagnose a gate or dispatch mismatch.

title: Pilot reports, Volanta evidence, and outcome analysis
definition: The server re-fetches Volanta and derives COMPLETED, DIVERTED, or INCOMPLETE plus reposition evidence.
why: The browser preview is untrusted and non-complete outcomes affect aircraft position and credit.
outcomes: Classify outcomes from evidence.
Choose reposition airport and required reason.

title: Review, credit, streaks, and aircraft lifecycle
definition: Approval limits eligible time, applies multipliers and streaks, updates pilot totals, moves aircraft, and may trigger inspection.
why: One decision changes several durable entities and must remain transactionally consistent.
outcomes: Calculate credited block and experience behavior.
Predict aircraft state after approval, rejection, or hard landing.

title: Schedule, hub health, administration, audit, and public news
definition: The timetable is deterministic and read-only; hub health is derived; owner tabs manage records; audit and org updates preserve traceability and communication.
why: Not every page is a CRUD screen and public/private communication shares one entity.
outcomes: Explain schedule and health derivation.
Map owner actions to audit and news visibility.

title: SimBrief generation, import, validation, and limits
definition: Generated URLs use D1, AIR callsign, BCS3, LIDO, and recovery zero payload; imports restrict host, path, size, time, and assignment match.
why: External planning data is useful only after provider and domain validation.
outcomes: Trace generated parameters.
Diagnose rejected route, type, format, or recovery payload.

title: Volanta evidence and VATSIM pre-file behavior
definition: Volanta public UUID data supplies verification; VATSIM is a browser link with an airDash remark and optional network record.
why: Provider fields have distinct authority and no API secret is stored.
outcomes: Distinguish Volanta evidence fields.
Explain VATSIM link generation and validation limits.

title: Notification history, polling, Web Push, and service worker
definition: Server-side history creates stable event records and read state; the push worker delivers pending records through VAPID subscriptions; the service worker handles display and click.
why: Browser-local state is not authoritative and failed subscriptions need lifecycle handling.
outcomes: Trace a notification from source row to click.
Diagnose missing, duplicate, or undelivered notifications.

title: CARTO, RainViewer, Google Fonts, and estimated map positions
definition: The browser contacts third-party tile and font providers; flight positions are estimated rather than telemetry.
why: Privacy, availability, API keys, and display claims differ for browser-side integrations.
outcomes: Identify direct browser requests.
Explain what the map can and cannot prove.

title: PowerPoint automation, liveries, GSX, and platform limits
definition: Windows scripts render and atomically replace the video; package builders create simulator content; some checks require private archives or an interactive desktop.
why: Source, deployed copies, hashes, interactive-session requirements, and unsupported automation must remain explicit.
outcomes: Trace the exporter and launcher.
Choose the valid platform-specific verification method.

title: Test purpose, categories, isolation, and current strategy
definition: Tests catch regressions and encode behavior; airDash combines pure unit scripts, syntax and type checks, smoke tests, builds, and manual visual checks.
why: The correct evidence depends on which boundary changed.
outcomes: Classify unit, integration, smoke, and visual checks.
Select validation by changed area.

title: Assertions, fixtures, fakes, and determinism
definition: Assertions compare expected and actual values; fixtures shape input; fakes replace dependencies; explicit time prevents flaky results.
why: A passing test should be reproducible and its failure should identify a contract.
outcomes: Read an assertion failure.
Design a deterministic project test.

title: API syntax and pure unit tests
definition: The check script parses all API files; two scripts cover streaks, outcomes, parsing, recovery, and gates without network or database.
why: Each command catches a different failure class and none proves route integration.
outcomes: State exactly what each script covers.
Interpret warning versus failure and exit code.

title: Type checking, isolated build, marker check, and visual check
definition: TypeScript checks contracts, Vite proves bundling, markers prove inclusion, and a browser proves rendered behavior.
why: No one check substitutes for the others and production site must not be the build target during validation.
outcomes: Run the sequence safely.
Diagnose missing marker or wrong working directory.

title: Smoke tests, coverage, CI gaps, and new test expectations
definition: A temporary API process exercises real startup and routes; route coverage and CI are absent; new pure logic needs deterministic assertions.
why: Evidence must disclose what was and was not automated, especially when a smoke test can migrate a database.
outcomes: Run a local smoke test safely.
Plan test and documentation changes for new behavior.

title: Symptom-first diagnosis and evidence order
definition: Troubleshooting begins from observable behavior, tests likely causes in priority order, and distinguishes before correcting.
why: Changing state before diagnosis can erase evidence or widen impact.
outcomes: Build a hypothesis tree from a symptom.
Choose read-only diagnostics first.

title: Health checks, logs, process state, and expected observations
definition: Health, direct listeners, PM2, containers, logs, and bundle hashes reveal distinct layers.
why: A green or red signal must be interpreted in its exact scope.
outcomes: Map a failing check to a component.
Read normal versus abnormal log lines.

title: Database outages, API startup failure, and PM2 restart limits
definition: The pg pool has no idle error handler, so a database restart crashes the API; repeated startup migration failure can exhaust PM2 restarts.
why: Operator recovery requires database readiness followed by explicit API state verification.
outcomes: Predict the observed failure sequence.
Recover without deleting data or restarting shared services blindly.

title: Authentication, origin, Vite, TypeScript, build, booking, and provider failures
definition: Similar user symptoms come from distinct boundaries and readable messages or status codes narrow the cause.
why: The correct fix differs between identity, origin, proxy path, type contract, concurrency, and external evidence.
outcomes: Distinguish common errors by output.
Select corrective action without bypassing a control.

title: Safe correction, verification, rollback, and escalation
definition: A corrective action states changes, risk, rollback, and verification; shared or destructive actions require owner confirmation.
why: Operational discipline prevents a local symptom from becoming a wider outage or data loss.
outcomes: Choose repair versus rollback versus escalation.
State final verification and remaining uncertainty.

title: Assets, threat surfaces, and trust boundaries
definition: Credentials, sessions, owner authority, personal data, operational integrity, downloads, and shared availability cross explicit trust boundaries.
why: Security starts by naming what must be protected and where trust changes.
outcomes: Classify project assets.
Map controls to boundary crossings.

title: Authentication, authorization, ownership, and CSRF defense
definition: The auth service identifies; middleware authorizes roles; SQL predicates enforce ownership; Origin rejects cross-site mutations.
why: Missing any one layer can expose another account or permit unwanted state change.
outcomes: Trace authenticated mutation defenses.
Review a new route for all authorization layers.

title: Secrets, session handling, and encryption boundaries
definition: Database and VAPID private credentials remain in untracked environment configuration; TLS terminates at Caddy; internal same-host traffic is plain.
why: Secrets must not enter Git, browser bundles, logs, or insecure copies, and encryption claims must match actual boundaries.
outcomes: Classify secret versus public identifier.
Plan rotation and state the transport boundary accurately.

title: Input validation, parameterized SQL, output encoding, headers, and dependency security
definition: Allow-lists, bounds, parameters, constraints, React escaping, headers, exact pins, locks, and audits provide layered controls.
why: Removing one layer turns untrusted data or third-party code into a direct risk.
outcomes: Review a field from request to rendering.
Evaluate a dependency or output change.

title: Audit, sensitive data, unsafe changes, reporting, and incident response
definition: Audit records actions but are not tamper-evident; data exposure differs by route; unsafe modifications and incidents require explicit response.
why: Security review includes visibility, evidence quality, containment, communication, and recovery.
outcomes: Classify route data exposure.
Respond to a suspected credential or owner compromise without public disclosure.

title: Environments, artifacts, release identity, and change classification
definition: Development and production are distinct; the changed area determines build, restart, backup, and procedure; commits and hashes identify a release.
why: Treating every change alike causes unnecessary outages or missing steps.
outcomes: Classify representative diffs.
Identify the deployed commit and frontend artifacts.

title: Pre-deployment validation, clean Git state, and rollback backup
definition: Production should deploy a merged clean commit after targeted validation and a verified release or database backup.
why: A clean source of truth and rollback point bound deployment risk.
outcomes: Apply the pre-deployment checklist.
Refuse deployment from an uncommitted or unvalidated tree.

title: Frontend, API, and combined deployment mechanics
definition: Frontend publication writes bind-mounted site artifacts without restart; API deployment restarts PM2; combined changes deploy API first.
why: Order protects clients that depend on new server fields and minimizes interruption.
outcomes: Trace each deployment side effect.
Select the correct combined order and verification.

title: Migration deployment and source-versus-schema rollback
definition: A smoke start can apply migrate; API source rollback does not remove columns, constraints, or data changes.
why: Schema changes carry durable risk beyond code rollback and require a database backup and planned reverse action.
outcomes: Plan a migration deployment.
Explain why improvised restore or source rollback is insufficient.

title: Static files, Nginx, Caddy, Windows automation, and post-deployment verification
definition: Each non-code artifact has a distinct cache, reload, blast radius, and validation procedure.
why: Shared configuration changes demand validation before reload and complete live verification afterward.
outcomes: Choose a static or configuration deployment procedure.
Apply health, marker, log, and visual verification.

title: Health, process, container, systemd, Git, and artifact state
definition: A complete session check combines HTTP, PM2, Docker, systemd, bundle, and Git observations.
why: No single health endpoint proves the entire deployment and source state.
outcomes: Run the read-only health inventory.
Interpret restarts versus unstable restarts.

title: Log sources, normal lines, and background-job verification
definition: PM2 and Docker capture different components; jobs have no success log and must be checked through data effects.
why: Absence of an error line is not evidence that a silent job ran.
outcomes: Find the right log.
Write a read-only query that proves each job effect.

title: Audit review, routine maintenance, disk, dependencies, PM2 persistence, and bundle cleanup
definition: Operators review durable actions and maintain backup, disk, dependency, process-list, and generated-artifact hygiene.
why: Small maintenance omissions accumulate into unrecoverable or confusing state.
outcomes: Plan a maintenance interval.
Remove stale bundles without breaking retained rollback.

title: Capacity, performance, metrics, traces, and alerting limits
definition: The single-process system has known bundle, query, pool, and scaling characteristics but no metrics, tracing, or automated alerting.
why: Operators must distinguish measured capacity from assumptions and disclose monitoring gaps.
outcomes: Explain current bottlenecks and pool limits.
Design a minimal external health alert without claiming existing telemetry.

title: Incident diagnosis, planned shutdown, startup, and escalation
definition: Incidents follow health, logs, dependency, recent-change, audit, correction, and verification order; shared restarts require coordination.
why: A consistent evidence sequence preserves availability and prevents random restart behavior.
outcomes: Execute the diagnosis order from a scenario.
Plan graceful whole-system maintenance and verify recovery.

title: State inventory, backup scope, and unreproducible assets
definition: Git, environment secrets, frontend artifacts, database data, downloads, profiles, Caddy, and PM2 state have different recovery sources.
why: A backup plan that omits secrets or operational downloads cannot rebuild the service.
outcomes: Map every state class to a recovery source.
Identify current backup gaps.

title: Release backups, database dumps, permissions, checksums, and verification
definition: Release backups copy active artifacts and API source with SHA-256; pg_dump custom format captures the schema and data and pg_restore --list verifies contents.
why: A backup is not trusted until its integrity and expected contents are checked.
outcomes: Explain each backup command and output.
Choose retention and privacy controls.

title: Destructive database restoration and rollback limits
definition: A clean schema restore replaces current airDash data and loses later records; it requires API stop, current-state backup, owner approval, restore, migration, and verification.
why: Restoration is not an exploratory undo command and source rollback cannot replace it.
outcomes: State every precondition and data-loss consequence.
Reject an improvised production restore.

title: PM2, static container, database container, Caddy, frontend, profiles, and download recovery
definition: Each component has an exact recovery procedure, dependencies, persistence location, and shared-impact boundary.
why: Recreating a stateless container differs from restoring shared database state or unreproducible files.
outcomes: Choose the correct component recovery.
Explain mounts, network, volume, and PM2 save behavior.

title: Complete-host disaster order, recovery point, recovery time, and proof limits
definition: A complete rebuild follows tools, Git, secrets, database, API, frontend, downloads, containers, Caddy, and health verification.
why: Order respects dependencies and exposes what cannot be reproduced from repository and database alone.
outcomes: Order the complete recovery.
State realistic recovery point and unresolved gaps.

title: Issue scope, prerequisites, and branch workflow
definition: A contributor agrees scope, starts from current release, creates one focused branch, and never commits directly to release.
why: Small isolated change reduces wasted work and review risk.
outcomes: Prepare a branch from current remote state.
Identify when an issue or owner agreement is required.

title: Coding standards and validation by change class
definition: API changes preserve validation, parameters, transactions, errors, audit, and tests; frontend changes preserve types, accessibility, styles, and build checks.
why: A diff is complete only when its implementation and evidence satisfy the owning area.
outcomes: Review a proposed code change.
Select and run the complete validation checklist.

title: Canonical documentation and maintenance triggers
definition: Routes, variables, schema, jobs, security boundaries, deployments, features, dependencies, and tests each trigger specific canonical updates.
why: Documentation drift is a product defect and coverage must remain connected to source evidence.
outcomes: Choose pages for a code change.
Update academy concept and assessment coverage with the canonical docs.

title: Specific staging, commit quality, pull-request evidence, review, and merge
definition: Only intended files are staged; commits explain why; the PR reports validation, docs, risk, rollback, and omissions; review responses use new commits.
why: Inspectable and attributable change is the delivery mechanism, especially without branch protection or CI.
outcomes: Prepare a safe commit and PR.
Respond to review without hiding history.

title: Guided contribution, capstone evidence, and professional limits
definition: Integrated evidence combines trace, implementation, tests, docs, validation, diff review, risk, rollback, incident diagnosis, and human explanation.
why: No score guarantees professional performance; durable confidence comes from delayed evidence plus independent reviewed work.
outcomes: Complete and explain the contribution exercise.
State the exact scope and limits of academy evidence.
